opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think sound and color are really the two canonical examples of what it means to have a sensory map, and they're useful precisely because they're so well understood.

With color, we've got a physical stimulus, which is light at different wavelengths, and then we've got perception. And what's remarkable is that we figured out, over a couple hundred years, a map that connects the two. Wavelength is a single physical dimension, but our perception of color isn't just a line. It wraps around into a color wheel, and you can add saturation and brightness, and you get these perceptual color spaces. The point is that the map tells you how things *look* relative to each other. Two colors that are close together in that space look similar to us. And once you have that map, you can do amazing things. You can build a monitor, you can build a camera, you can print a photograph, because you understand the relationship between the physics and the perception well enough to reproduce it.

Sound is similar. There's a physical quantity, frequency, and there's a perceptual quantity, pitch. And again, the relationship isn't trivial. Pitch is roughly logarithmic in frequency, and octaves sound "the same" in a certain way, which is why a piano keyboard repeats. So the map has structure that reflects how our brains process the signal, not just the raw physics.

What a sensory map really represents, then, is a coordinate system for perception. It says: here are the axes along which things vary for a human perceiver, and here's how distance in this space corresponds to perceived similarity. And the thing that's so striking is that for smell we didn't have that. We had no equivalent of the color wheel or the piano keyboard. Molecules are high-dimensional, the relationship between structure and odor is incredibly nonlinear, and small changes to a molecule can completely change how it smells. So the question we've been working on is: can we build that map for olfaction, using machine learning, the way physicists and psychologists built it for vision and hearing? Because if you can, you unlock the same kinds of things: predicting what a new molecule will smell like, designing new scents, and eventually maybe digitizing smell the way we digitized color and sound.

r001.rationale: The response says frequency relates to perceived pitch and that pitch is roughly logarithmic in frequency, but it does not describe a sound map as a single low-to-high frequency axis.

r002.rationale: It mentions wavelength, saturation, and brightness, but does not connect three numerical color coordinates to the eye’s three channels of color information.

r003.rationale: It presents sound and color as canonical examples of sensory maps, without noting that vision and hearing each admit multiple maps.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that for most of our senses, we actually have a map. And what I mean by a map is a way of relating stimuli to each other, a geometry, where things that are close together in the map are perceived as similar and things that are far apart are perceived as different.

So take color. If I give you a wavelength of light, say 650 nanometers, you'll see red. If I give you 450 nanometers, you'll see blue. And there's a smooth, continuous relationship in between. We know this so well that we have a color wheel, we have RGB coordinates, and I can send you a hex code and you'll render exactly the color I'm seeing. We didn't always have that. It took Newton with the prism, and then a couple hundred years of work by people like Maxwell and Helmholtz, to figure out that this enormously rich perceptual experience could be described with basically three numbers. And once you have that, you can build all kinds of technology on top of it. Cameras, displays, printers, everything about how we reproduce visual experience depends on having that map.

Sound is the same story. There's frequency, there's amplitude, and we know that if you double the frequency you get the same note an octave higher. That's a map. Musicians have been exploiting that structure for thousands of years, and it's the reason we can record a sound, compress it, send it across the world, and play it back and it sounds like the original.

Now, the thing that struck me is that for smell, we have nothing like that. There's no color wheel for scent. If I hand you a molecule, there's no existing theory that lets you predict what it's going to smell like. There's no notion of distance, where I could say this molecule and that molecule are five units apart in odor space. And without that map, you can't digitize the sense. You can't do for smell what the microphone and the camera did for hearing and vision.

So that's really the framing for me. Sound and color show you what's possible once you have a map. They show you that you can go from this incredibly subjective, personal experience to something quantitative, something you can build engineering on. And smell is the sense where that work hasn't been done yet.

r001.rationale: The response mentions frequency and octave relationships, but does not describe sound’s map as a single low-to-high frequency axis.

r002.rationale: It says color can be described with three numbers and mentions RGB, but does not connect those coordinates to the eye’s three channels of color information.

r003.rationale: The response presents a map for color and a map for sound, without noting that vision and hearing each admit multiple sensory maps.

astra-6.text:
I think sound and color are useful examples because we understand their maps pretty well. With sound, you have frequency: as you move along that axis, a tone goes from low to high. That gives you a relationship between a physical property of the stimulus and what you experience.

Color is a little more interesting. Light has a spectrum, but our eyes compress that spectrum through three types of cone cells. So the map of color is really a map of what our visual system can distinguish. Two different spectra can look like the same color.

The key idea is that a sensory map organizes stimuli according to perception. Things that are nearby should feel similar, and moving through the map should correspond to a predictable change in your experience. It’s not just a catalog of wavelengths or molecules; it’s a way of connecting what’s out in the world to what happens in your head.

r001.rationale: It describes sound frequency as an axis where tones go from low to high.

r002.rationale: It mentions three cone-cell types, but does not connect them to three numerical coordinates used to represent color.

r003.rationale: It describes sensory maps generally but does not say that vision and hearing each admit multiple maps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think sound and color give us an intuition for what a sensory map should do. With sound, you have frequency: as you move along that axis, a pitch gets higher or lower. Sounds that are close together on that axis sound similar. With color, you need more dimensions, but the idea is the same: nearby points should look similar, and moving through the space should produce a predictable change in what you perceive.

So a sensory map is a way of organizing a subjective experience into a space where distance means something. It gives you a way to say not just that two things are different, but how they’re related.

r001.rationale: It describes sound as organized along a frequency axis, where pitch gets higher or lower as you move along it.

r002.rationale: It says color needs more dimensions but does not connect three numerical coordinates to the eye’s three color-information channels.

r003.rationale: It describes sensory maps generally, but does not say that vision and hearing each admit multiple maps.
